title: Ezekiel 16:35–43
context: The LORD pronounces judgment on Jerusalem. Because of her idolatry and the blood of her children, he will gather the very nations she courted, and they will turn against her, strip away her wealth, and destroy her shrines and houses. The allegory describes the judgment in the terms of the law's penalties for adultery and bloodshed, and in the terms of a siege and its aftermath. The LORD's purpose is to end her unfaithfulness and bring his wrath to rest. The section closes by repeating that she did not remember the days of her youth. These notes keep the descriptions of judgment and violence sober and non-graphic.

verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls Jerusalem to hear his word. Arminian readers see him calling the city to account in the language of the allegory, as the charge gives way to the sentence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word “Therefore” links the judgment directly to the sins described. The LORD speaks as judge, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: ‘The Lord GOD says, “Because your filthiness was poured out, and your nakedness uncovered through your prostitution with your lovers; and because of all the idols of your abominations, and for the blood of your children, that you gave to them;
verses.arminianNotes: “The Lord GOD says.” Arminian readers see the grounds of judgment summarized: idolatry and the bloodshed of her children. The judgment answers real guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the charges combine unfaithfulness to the LORD and violence against the innocent. Both traditions see justice, not arbitrary anger, in the verdict.

verses.text: therefore see, I will gather all your lovers, with whom you have taken pleasure, and all those whom you have loved, with all those whom you have hated. I will even gather them against you on every side, and will uncover your nakedness to them, that they may see all your nakedness.
verses.arminianNotes: “therefore see, I will gather all your lovers.” Arminian readers see the nations Jerusalem trusted becoming the means of her judgment, gathered “against you on every side.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself gathers the nations. The public exposure in the allegory pictures Jerusalem's shame before the world, which these notes leave in its symbolic setting.

verses.text: I will judge you as women who break wedlock and shed blood are judged; and I will bring on you the blood of wrath and jealousy.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will judge you as women who break wedlock and shed blood are judged.” Arminian readers see the judgment matched to the two charges of unfaithfulness and bloodshed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “the blood of wrath and jealousy” shows the LORD's covenant jealousy. His jealousy is not petty but the zeal of a faithful partner betrayed.

verses.text: I will also give you into their hand, and they will throw down your vaulted place, and break down your lofty places. They will strip you of your clothes and take your beautiful jewels. They will leave you naked and bare.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will also give you into their hand.” Arminian readers see the nations throwing down Jerusalem's shrines and taking her wealth, so that she ends where she began, without the covering he had given her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of verse 7. The gifts of verses 10–14 are taken away, showing that what the LORD gave can be removed when it is misused.

verses.text: They will also bring up a company against you, and they will stone you with stones, and thrust you through with their swords.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will also bring up a company against you.” Arminian readers see the allegory merge with the reality of invasion: an assembled force carrying out judgment on the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the penalties echo the law's judgments and also describe a siege. The violence is not dwelt on here, but the seriousness of covenant breaking is in view.

verses.text: They will burn your houses with fire, and execute judgments on you in the sight of many women. I will cause you to cease from playing the prostitute, and you will also give no hire any more.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will burn your houses with fire.” Arminian readers see the city's destruction carried out “in the sight of many women,” that is, before the nations. The LORD will end her unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the promise that the LORD will put an end to her unfaithfulness. Judgment has a purpose: to put an end to the sin. Both traditions see that purpose here.

verses.text: So I will cause my wrath toward you to rest, and my jealousy will depart from you. I will be quiet, and will not be angry any more.
verses.arminianNotes: “So I will cause my wrath toward you to rest.” Arminian readers see that the LORD's anger is not endless. When justice is done, his jealousy departs and he will “be quiet.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD's wrath has a measure and an end. This prepares for the promise of mercy in verses 60–63, while the context here is still judgment.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Because you have not remembered the days of your youth, but have raged against me in all these things; therefore, behold, I also will bring your way on your head,” says the Lord GOD: “and you shall not commit this lewdness with all your abominations.
verses.arminianNotes: “Because you have not remembered the days of your youth.” Arminian readers see the LORD returning to the root problem and bringing Jerusalem's “way on your head” as just recompense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this repeats verse 22. Forgetting grace led to rebellion, and the judgment fits the conduct. Remembrance will return as a key theme in verses 60–63.
